content.one_sentence_role: Cancels the Hessian terms that arise when differentiating a cofactor row.
content.natural_language_statement:
Let $H:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be $C^2$, and fix $i\in\{1,\ldots,n\}$. Let $e_j$ be the $j$th standard coordinate vector, with coordinates $(e_j)_q=\delta_{jq}$. Define the scalar coordinate maps and the derivative matrix by
$$H_k(x):=(H(x))_k,\qquad A(x)_{kq}:=\partial_qH_k(x).$$
Thus rows are output coordinates and columns are differentiation directions. Let $F:\mathbb R^n\to\mathbb R^n$ be the fixed $i$th cofactor row field:
$$F_j(x):=(F(x))_j=\det\bigl(A(x)[i\leftarrow e_j^{\mathsf T}]\bigr),\qquad
F(x)=C_i(A(x)).$$
Then, at every $x$,
$$\operatorname{div}F(x):=\sum_{j=1}^n\partial_jF_j(x)=0.$$
content.assumptions: The hypothesis is twice continuous differentiability on the whole coordinate space. There is no invertibility, compact-support, or boundary assumption. A row $i$ is supplied; the zero-dimensional case consequently has no row to check.
content.conclusion: Every cofactor row field of the derivative is divergence-free, pointwise. The input and output coordinate indices remain distinct in the cancellation below.
content.proof_summary: Differentiate one coordinate $F_j(x)=\det(A(x)[i\leftarrow e_j^{\mathsf T}])$ first. Rowwise differentiation and row multilinearity express it using $\partial_j\partial_qH_k$. In the divergence sum, the terms indexed by $(j,q)$ and $(q,j)$ cancel: their second derivatives agree and their two-row determinants have opposite signs.

proof_steps.text:
**Differentiate one cofactor coordinate, not the whole divergence at once.** Write the $k$th row of $A(x)$ as
$$r_k(x)=\bigl(\partial_1H_k(x),\ldots,\partial_nH_k(x)\bigr).$$
For fixed $j$,
$$F_j(x)=\det\bigl(r_1(x),\ldots,r_{i-1}(x),e_j^{\mathsf T},r_{i+1}(x),\ldots,r_n(x)\bigr).$$
Only the rows $r_k(x)$ with $k\ne i$ vary. The finite product rule in the determinant expansion therefore gives
$$\partial_jF_j(x)=\sum_{k\ne i}
\det\!\left((A(x)[i\leftarrow e_j^{\mathsf T}])
[k\leftarrow\partial_j r_k(x)]\right).$$
This is the rowwise derivative formula: each summand differentiates just one nonconstant row. The $C^2$ assumption makes every row being differentiated a $C^1$ map.

**Expand the differentiated row and then take the divergence.** The coordinate row satisfies
$$\partial_jr_k(x)=\bigl(\partial_j\partial_qH_k(x)\bigr)_{q=1}^n
=\sum_{q=1}^n\partial_j\partial_qH_k(x)\,e_q^{\mathsf T}.$$
Define, displaying both replaced rows,
$$B_{ikjq}(x):=(A(x)[i\leftarrow e_j^{\mathsf T}])[k\leftarrow e_q^{\mathsf T}].$$
Linearity of the determinant in row $k$ turns Step 1 into
$$\partial_jF_j(x)=\sum_{k\ne i}\sum_{q=1}^n
\partial_j\partial_qH_k(x)\det B_{ikjq}(x).$$
Finally sum over $j$ and reorder these finite sums:
$$\operatorname{div}F(x)=\sum_{k\ne i}\sum_{j=1}^n\sum_{q=1}^n
\partial_j\partial_qH_k(x)\det B_{ikjq}(x).$$

**Identify the two symmetries.** For each fixed $k\ne i$, equality of mixed second derivatives gives
$$\partial_j\partial_qH_k(x)=\partial_q\partial_jH_k(x).$$
The matrices $B_{ikjq}(x)$ and $B_{ikqj}(x)$ differ by interchanging rows $i$ and $k$: these rows are $e_j^{\mathsf T},e_q^{\mathsf T}$ in the first and $e_q^{\mathsf T},e_j^{\mathsf T}$ in the second. Hence
$$\det B_{ikjq}(x)=-\det B_{ikqj}(x).$$
For $j=q$, the two rows coincide and each determinant is zero. There is no matrix-invertibility hypothesis in either step.

**Perform the cancellation.** For a fixed $k\ne i$, call the inner finite sum $S_k(x)$. Relabel $j$ and $q$, and then use Step 3:
$$\begin{aligned}
S_k(x)&:=\sum_{j,q}\partial_j\partial_qH_k(x)\det B_{ikjq}(x)\\
&=\sum_{j,q}\partial_q\partial_jH_k(x)\det B_{ikqj}(x)\\
&=-\sum_{j,q}\partial_j\partial_qH_k(x)\det B_{ikjq}(x)=-S_k(x).
\end{aligned}$$
Thus $2S_k(x)=0$ over $\mathbb R$, so $S_k(x)=0$. Substitution into Step 2 gives $\operatorname{div}F(x)=\sum_{k\ne i}S_k(x)=0$.

content.lean_realization_notes: Here $H_k$ and $F_j$ are scalar functions, whereas $H$ and $F$ are vector-valued maps. For any $C^1$ vector field $V$, $\partial_jV_j(x)=(DV(x)e_j)_j$. Thus taking the derivative in direction $e_j$ and then taking coordinate $j$ is precisely the $j$th term in the divergence.
